# Second-generation pulse design: tamper and lower-energy inflow study ✨

Compare tampers and lower-energy inflows in the hydrogen-enriched, staged CNO pulse design. The aim is to improve confinement and reduce prepared energy per completed helium nucleus while retaining a positive whole-cycle energy and material balance. Smaller pulses remain a separate design goal. The tamper concepts and lower-energy inflows are proposed candidates; no tampered pulse or selected-mixture low-energy inflow has yet been simulated for this study.

## Weekend sprint: geometry first

The first task is to test whether the stated pulse profiles can be assembled from the distributed source, starting with the existing conservative untamped reference. Then evaluate the proposed slower inflow and following-layer geometry. Geometry screens precede the large pulse-gain and tamper-material sweeps; a prescribed one-dimensional pulse remains a physics control until its assembly assumptions have been tested.

1. **Reconstruct the reference.** Extract the actual source-outlet positions or their documented angular model, receiver radius, launch windows, radial speed and density profiles, packet sizes, source/neutralization constraints and target state. Distinguish physical transport columns from effective merger regions. Identify assumptions that are specified, inferred or still missing, including the earlier central-seed concept and slow tail. Use the selected profiles and existing source calculations rather than a single illustrative speed.
2. **Trace delivery.** Build a time-dependent geometry screen from the source to contact and central compression, using finite packet/stream lengths and angular footprint. Plot or tabulate radial position versus time, occupancy of channels, approach and crossing events, momentum directions and arrival order. Screen the untamped reference, reduced-speed profiles and fuel-first following layers. Add gapped or dynamically formed layers only with explicit trajectories and closure models. Include free-flight controls, conservation checks, independently reproduced flight times and clearly stated simplifications.
3. **Test the geometric gates.** Establish whether the required mass can be delivered to the stated radii with the desired ordering, coverage and arrival windows; detect path intersections and distinguish intentional contact from unmodeled interpenetration. Evaluate angular gaps, source aperture and column overlap, crossing and closure, core expansion by layer arrival, finite packet spread and collisions with prior-pulse tails. Compare timing, positioning, velocity dispersion and merger requirements with documented source constraints. Sweep uncertain parameters and state which assumptions control any pass or failure; calculate a sensitivity-derived tolerance rather than assigning one in advance.
4. **Carry forward viable candidates.** Record mass flow, launch energy, required ports and timing, mapped density/velocity/temperature/composition, and unresolved contact or shock physics. A geometry screen supplies necessary conditions, not proof of a realizable source or symmetric burn. Only then run the corresponding hydrodynamics and paired tamper comparisons, keeping speculative starting profiles labeled as controls. If no geometry passes, document the obstruction and revise the source or pulse architecture before expanding the gain sweep.

The sprint deliverable is an auditable geometry report with trajectories, equations, input provenance, failures and parameter sensitivities; distinguish exact kinematic results from assumed interactions and any subjective 80% credible interval. Follow with the lower-energy and tamper calculations only for the geometries that clear the first screen.

## Motivation and baseline

The existing second-generation mixture and component design uses staged, optically thick, prescribed converging pulses, with a 30 m reference radius for the major pulses. See [mixture design](/home/tkwa/.codex/worktrees/protium-fusion/website/docs/protium-fusion/mixture-design/README.md), [pulse methods](/home/tkwa/.codex/worktrees/protium-fusion/website/docs/protium-fusion/mixture-design/methods.md), and [component design](/home/tkwa/.codex/worktrees/protium-fusion/website/docs/protium-fusion/component-design/README.md). Radius in these calculations is a reference scale, not the outer radius of the evolving fuel.

A new 64-zone radius sensitivity used the earlier N14 + p stage, full reaction network, corrected compression-cap viscosity and the prescribed 30 m hot inflow. Each run scaled every initial radius while preserving the initial density, temperature, composition and velocity profile. The fuel input energy consequently scales as radius cubed. The model uses LTE and a constant gray opacity of 0.001 m²/kg. It is a comparison for motivating a tamper, not a run of the selected enriched fuel and not a result for a tampered capsule.

| Reference radius | Outer radius near peak temperature | Fuel mass | Capture product per initial N14 | Prompt capture nuclear energy / fuel input |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 30 m | 77.8 m | 1.131e13 kg | 0.5394 | 8.196 |
| 10 m | 20.8 m | 4.189e11 kg | 0.2174 | 3.304 |
| 3 m | 6.56 m | 1.131e10 kg | 0.005853 | 0.08895 |
| 1.5 m | 3.25 m | 1.414e9 kg | 0.002141 | 0.03253 |

The 3 m run still has a naive center-to-surface Thomson optical depth of approximately 4.5e6 near its maximum sampled temperature. The decline in capture yield therefore cannot be attributed to low scattering depth alone. A shorter hydrodynamic time and a changed temperature and density history are plausible reasons; the sweep does not isolate their individual contributions. The local free–free absorption depth of about 825 quoted in discussion was a half-cell diagnostic at the 30 m baseline's hottest point, not a requirement for the complete pulse.

The 30 m case is the previously saved corrected-viscosity regression. The 10 m, 3 m and 1.5 m cases were run for four reference sound times with relative tolerance 1e-6 and absolute tolerance 1e-11; all reported completion, with energy residuals below 1.5e-7 of initial energy. The 30 m regression used relative tolerance 1e-7. These single-resolution outputs do not establish convergence or a realizable cold driver. The saved [probe](radius_probe.py), JSON results and spatial traces in this directory preserve the new runs; the probe depends on the existing research worktree, its input profile and numerical environment. No energy from subsequent beta decay is included in the stated capture-stage ratio.

A subsequent fixed-profile [larger-radius screen](../larger-pulse-screen/README.md) gives Q = 8.97, 9.50 and 10.21 at 45, 60 and 90 m, respectively, for the same earlier N14 mixture; the 30 m reference is 8.20. These single-resolution runs increase prepared energy with mass and do not test a lower-energy inflow. Their modest gain increase motivates a joint size and energy search rather than a radius-only extrapolation. The selected enriched N14 stage is a separate baseline.

## Lower-energy inflow and size survey

Begin with the selected hydrogen-enriched N14 stage and its actual saved precursor profile. Retain the earlier N14 profile as a regression control. Explore reference radii 3, 10, 30, 60 and 90 m and multiply the inward velocity profile by 0.5, 0.65, 0.8 and 1.0. These are search points; refine the region where burn and gain change sharply. Scale radius at fixed initial density, composition and temperature for the initial comparison. Hold the original thermal profile fixed when changing velocity, calculate kinetic and internal energy separately from the full profile, and record the resulting total prepared energy. The squared velocity factor applies to kinetic energy only. Identify the physical source profile and its reference energy explicitly; do not carry a fixed-energy or entropy-floor adjustment into this sweep without charging it.

At each radius include the unmodified, untamped reference and compare lower-speed runs at the same fuel mass and composition. At fixed prepared energy, compare independently specified profiles and report differences in their fuel state and mass; do not silently rescale a case to claim an equal-energy comparison. Use a physical end time long enough to capture expansion and the relevant yield and energy partition, with a duration-extension check; report the same diagnostic milestones across cases. Follow output composition through beta decay and the existing cycle ledger. Record failed, incomplete and numerically guarded runs as well as completed cases.

For the joint survey, pair each promising lower-speed inflow with an untamped control and the prioritized fuel-liner, carbon-rich and hydrogen-rich cases below. Sweep shell-to-fuel mass ratio, shell speed and arrival timing as specified below. Compare first at identical fuel state to isolate shell effects, then at equal **total** prepared energy including the shell. Also compare the full configurations at equal fuel mass and against the same-radius untamped baseline so that an apparent gain cannot be attributed to an omitted shell or preparation cost. Determine the range of size and energy budgets before expanding the full cross-product.

## Delivering the outer layer

The initial concentric layer in a one-dimensional calculation is an objective for the source design, not an established delivery method. A slower outer layer launched early from the same receiver can arrive close in time to a faster core, but it will initially lie farther inward. For the core to end up inside it, their paths must cross or the material must be routed through gaps before the layer closes. This creates a three-dimensional collision, mixing and timing problem.

Screen a same-speed or faster following layer as the first delivery concept. Launch the fuel first; launch the layer later on the same inward paths, timed to remain behind the fuel and arrive shortly after it. Account for the layer's actual kinetic energy and its interaction with the decelerating and rebounding fuel; a faster layer is not automatically a lower-energy system. A slower core and a following layer of comparable speed can still reduce the fuel's energy relative to the original high-speed reference.

As a second concept, evaluate separate angular delivery channels: the fuel uses openings in an incomplete layer, which closes behind it. Compute aperture coverage, packet or jet paths, interactions, closure symmetry, deposition and radiation leakage. Do not assume the existing source outlets automatically provide clean channels or a continuous shell. As a third concept, study forming a shaped outer layer dynamically from staged fuel flow; require the starting flow and shocks to emerge from a specified source trajectory. A preassembled concentric configuration is a useful hydrodynamic control only until an assembly path is specified.

For each concept, provide a space-time plot or equivalent trajectory table from source outlet to layer closure, including launch order, speeds, finite packet sizes and fuel/shell surfaces. Test for trajectory crossings, collisions and the actual time and radius at which the fuel is enclosed. Couple the resulting density, composition, temperature and velocity fields to the pulse simulation. Propagate path and timing errors into measurable nonuniformity and gain; establish tolerances by sensitivity analysis instead of assigning a guessed microsecond requirement. Include launch, steering, shell kinetic and thermal energy, apertures and assembly equipment in the same system ledger.

Carry promising cases into the selected N15, C12 and C13 stages, including their own source profiles and physical compositions, and recompute the coupled material routing. Larger pulses can change timing, peak and stored driver energy, receiver loading and inventory. Recalculate those constraints rather than assuming the original plant scales unchanged.

## Whole-cycle gain target

The selected plant ledger gives 24.716 MeV of non-neutrino nuclear energy and 1.937 MeV of prepared pulse energy per net helium nucleus, or whole-cycle Q = 12.76. With nuclear yield per helium held at 24.716 MeV, Q = 50 requires at most 0.4943 MeV of total prepared energy per helium, a 74.5% reduction. This is a research target, not a demonstrated result. Recompute the numerator for actual isotope outcomes and escaped neutrino energy; charge every fuel and tamper stage, including precursor preparation, once.

An initial milestone is a factor-of-two reduction in prepared energy per net helium at useful conversion and a closed positive whole-plant electric balance. The Q = 50 criterion is assessed on the completed whole-cycle ledger, not on any individual prompt stage. Preserve the distinction between prepared-energy gain and electrical gain: driver efficiency, captured outgoing energy, sorting, auxiliary loads, refurbishment and the heat cycle belong in the plant account and must not be double-counted.

## Candidate configurations

Choose the material from comparative calculations; no best tamper has yet been demonstrated. Prioritize constituents already present in the fuel cycle and recovery system. Compare each with an untamped control. Define initial mass, pressure, density, radial velocity and composition throughout each layer; assemble them before peak compression and evolve the entire fuel–tamper system. Keep the initial fuel profile fixed for a first mechanism comparison, then compare again at equal **total** delivered energy including the tamper.

1. **Staged CNO–hydrogen inflow — first candidate.** Retain an outer, cooler layer based on the same stage's fuel mixture. Its inward momentum may confine the core and the layer may itself react or return to the fuel loop. Track its full burn and recovery separately; its altered temperature, density and arrival time can also change mixing and shock dynamics.
2. **Carbon-rich layer — second candidate.** Test carbon-12-rich material and a carbon–hydrogen mixture compatible with the existing carbon return and catcher systems. Carbon can participate in proton captures, alter the isotope routing and change radiation transport; account for its energy, downstream processing and possible catalyst losses. Specify the isotope composition and material state rather than assuming cold graphite properties hold during the pulse.
3. **Hydrogen-rich layer — comparison candidate.** Test a proton-rich outer layer whose material can enter the existing hydrogen return stream. Its lower mass density and altered equation of state may make it less effective at a specified geometry; evaluate actual layer density, inertia, compressibility and preparation cost. A dense hydrogen layer is a modeled state that needs an assembly route, not an assumed cold solid shell.
4. **Helium-4 layer — optional comparator.** Test recovered helium only if a CNO-compatible layer fails or if the helium case offers a useful confinement comparison. It is a low-Z byproduct that needs its own compression, storage, recovery and return costs. Include alpha-induced reactions relevant to the modeled temperatures and composition; extend or bound the network where necessary.

If those candidates do not provide sufficient confinement, screen other materials based on calculated hot-state opacity, equation of state, confinement, nuclear side reactions, recoverability and preparation cost. High-Z options can be evaluated when a specific mechanism justifies them. Use the same criteria for every material and retain unsuccessful or uncertain results. Cold tabulated properties serve only as preparation references.

For the initial survey, use shell-to-fuel mass ratios 0, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3 and 1 as exploration points, plus at least two choices of shell inward speed and arrival timing. These are search points, not recommended specifications or probability intervals. Evaluate the selected nitrogen capture mixture first at 3 m and 10 m reference radii alongside the 30 m untamped case and the larger-radius lower-energy survey. Then transfer promising ideas to the other reaction stages.

## Screening calculation

For intuition only, a thin shell initially at rest under constant pressure satisfies Δr ≈ p t²/(2Σ), with Σ the mass per unit area. At p=1e18 Pa, t=5 µs and Δr=2 m, Σ≈6.25e6 kg/m²; assigning that column at 6.56 m radius gives ≈3.4e9 kg, about 30% of the 3 m fuel mass. Pressure was selected from the untamped outermost resolved cell near peak temperature; neither that pressure nor a stationary thin shell describes the evolving interface. The required column is large enough that geometric thickness and material state must be calculated for each candidate. This calculation is a parameter-scale prompt, not a physical mass prediction or bounds on required confinement.

An illustrative kinetic-energy scale for 3.4e9 kg at 1e6 m/s is 1.7e21 J, compared with 3.493e22 J of fuel input in the 3 m untamped control. Count the tamper's actual initial kinetic and thermal energy, compression work, driver inefficiency, subsequent product recovery, and material processing. Some outgoing energy may be recovered; do not assume a recovery fraction or count it twice.

## Required model and decision criteria

- Add distinct fuel, buffer and tamper materials to radiation hydrodynamics with material-specific EOS, opacity and electron/ion thermodynamics. Resolve interfaces and follow changing ionization and radiation transport; benchmark the coupled solver against shock-tube and energy-conservation controls. A gray LTE survey is a first screen, followed by frequency-dependent transport at consequential boundaries.
- Record fuel density and temperature histories, interface pressure and velocity, shock timing, burn fraction, escaped radiation and particle energy. Compare paired runs both at fixed fuel state and fixed total input. Repeat at multiple zoning and timestep settings and retain failed or stopped runs.
- Model or bound interface instability and material transport; every admixture changes composition, dilution, heat capacity and radiation transport. Evaluate the hot ionization state and opacity for each material. In an opaque pulse, emitted radiation may be reabsorbed or redistributed; use radiation transport instead of treating emission as immediate escape. Two- or three-dimensional instability and assembly work are required before claiming a feasible configuration.
- Compute prompt stage gain as nuclear energy less explicitly escaped weak energy divided by **fuel plus tamper preparation and delivery energy**. Account separately for captured outgoing energy, delayed beta decays, catalyst return, additional processing and electrical efficiencies in the whole-cycle ledger. Do not promote a capture-stage ratio to net electric gain.
- The exploratory 3 m control converts 0.5853% of N14 with a prompt capture nuclear/input ratio of 0.08895. If energy release per conversion remains approximately constant, approximately 6.6% conversion would yield a ratio of one against the *old fuel-only* input. The tamper adds costs, so this is a diagnostic threshold, not the plant break-even condition.
- Recompute pulse mass, frequency, collection load, chemical/isotope handling and mass replacement for the second-generation plant. Check whether a lower fuel pulse mass survives the cost of tamper inventory and a higher firing rate. Revisit the other reaction stages and their waiting-point inventories.

For lower-energy inflows, the immediate acceptance criterion is a converged increase in prompt capture-stage gain over the same-radius untamped reference with lower total prepared fuel-plus-shell energy, while explicitly reporting conversion and all energy channels. For tampers, also require the paired equal-total-energy comparison to show higher gain than the untamped control. Both paths then require a closed whole-cycle energy and material account, including source and plant constraints. Report subjective 80% credible intervals only when assumptions and evidence support calibration; no credible interval is assigned to these untested candidates.

## External references

- [Sandia, inertial confinement fusion and metal liners](https://www.sandia.gov/pulsed-power/inertial-confinement/).
- [NIST elemental material densities](https://physics.nist.gov/PhysRefData/XrayMassCoef/tab1.html) and [X-ray attenuation data](https://www.nist.gov/pml/x-ray-mass-attenuation-coefficients); cold-material references only.
- [Fuel–shell mix and fusion performance](https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1172490).

# Larger pulse radius screen

Runs on 2026-11-02 using `output/second-generation-tamper/radius_probe.py` and the same earlier N14-stage control, initial profile, 64 zones, full 27-isotope network, gray opacity 0.001 m²/kg, compression-cap viscosity, rtol 1e-6, atol 1e-11 and four reference sound times as the prior small-radius sweep. Runtime: Python 3.10 with `/tmp/protium-python`, one OpenBLAS thread. The 30 m comparison is the saved earlier regression (rtol 1e-7). Radius scales the initial profile at fixed density, temperature, composition and velocity; pulse mass and prepared energy scale as radius cubed. Prompt Q is deposited nuclear energy divided by fuel input energy, excluding subsequent beta decay and all driver/plant losses.

| Reference radius (m) | Mass (kg) | N14 conversion / initial catalyst | Prompt Q | Energy residual / initial energy |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 30 | 1.131e13 | 0.5394 | 8.196 | earlier regression |
| 45 | 3.817e13 | 0.5901193 | 8.96758 | 2.08e-6 |
| 60 | 9.048e13 | 0.6248556 | 9.49544 | 1.30e-6 |
| 90 | 3.054e14 | 0.6716260 | 10.20618 | -2.78e-6 |

All three new runs report success and final-time termination. JSON files preserve solver records and NPZ files the sampled traces. Single-resolution exploratory runs, with an older N14 composition: they do not predict the selected four-stage plant Q. The model prescribes a spherical hot converging inflow; source assembly, multidimensional effects, detailed radiation transport and material recovery are unresolved. Larger pulse impacts on the receiver and plant must be re-evaluated. See the [prior tamper and radius study](../second-generation-tamper/TAMPER-STUDY.md).
